```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)
library(simling)
library(broom)

source("slides_setup.R", local = knitr::knit_global())

options(width = 70, pillar.print_min = 4, pillar.print_max = 4)

words <- megastudy
m <- lm(rt ~ aoa, data = words)
b0 <- coef(m)[1]
b1 <- coef(m)[2]
r2 <- glance(m)$r.squared
```

# Transforming variables

<style>
  :root {
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the blue whale is the [largest animal]{.hl} known to have lived. The biggest accurately measured one, a female, was 29.5 m long and weighed 180 tonnes.

_Sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica; WWF_
:::

## Today

- Why we transform variables
- Linear transformations: units, centring, standardising
- Correlation: Pearson's r, and what it hides
- Logarithms: for predictors and for outcomes
- A note on the word "normalising"

## Data from {simling}

From today, most examples use data sets from `{simling}`, which you met in tutorial 1. The data are simulated, so we know the true effects.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(simling)
?megastudy
```

. . .

`megastudy`: item norms for 6000 words, as in large lexical decision megastudies. One row per word, with its mean reaction time (`rt`, in ms) and its age of acquisition (`aoa`, in years).

## Age of acquisition and reaction time

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.4
ggplot(words, aes(x = aoa, y = rt)) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, alpha = 0.15, size = 1) +
  labs(x = "Age of acquisition (years)", y = "Reaction time (ms)")
```

Each point is one of the 6000 words. Words learned later tend to take longer to recognise, and the cloud of points is roughly straight, so a linear model is a reasonable start.

## A simple regression

```{r}
words <- megastudy
m <- lm(rt ~ aoa, data = words)
tidy(m)[, 1:3]
```

. . .

Each extra year of age of acquisition goes with responses `r round(b1, 1)` ms slower, and a word learned at age 0 would take `r round(b0)` ms.

. . .

The model is fine, but its intercept describes a word learned at birth, far outside the data. Today we fix that, and change the scale of the slope, without touching the fit.

## Why transform?

| Goal | Example | Transformation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Coefficients that are easier to read | slope per month, intercept for a word of average age of acquisition | units, centring |
| Predictors on a common scale | age of acquisition (years) against word length (letters) | standardising |
| A shape the linear model can handle | skewed reaction times, word frequencies | logarithm |

. . .

Changing units, centring and standardising relabel the axis and leave the shape of the data as it is. The logarithm changes the shape as well.

## Linear vs non-linear {.smaller}

A [linear]{.hl} transformation adds, subtracts, multiplies or divides by a constant. A non-linear one, such as the logarithm, changes the shape of the distribution.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.0
rt <- tibble(rt_ms = zipf_rt$rt)

bind_rows(
  tibble(scale = "Milliseconds", value = rt$rt_ms),
  tibble(scale = "Seconds (÷ 1000)", value = rt$rt_ms / 1000),
  tibble(scale = "z-score", value = as.numeric(scale(rt$rt_ms))),
  tibble(scale = "log(milliseconds)", value = log(rt$rt_ms))
) |>
  mutate(scale = fct_inorder(scale),
         type = if_else(scale == "log(milliseconds)", "non-linear", "linear")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = type)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, colour = floor_col) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(linear = kingfisher, `non-linear` = hornbill)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count", fill = NULL)
```

Reaction times from `zipf_rt` on four scales. The three linear ones are the same histogram with different numbers on the axis. Only the log changes the shape.

# Linear transformations

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` a nursing blue whale calf gains up to 90 kg a day: that is 3.75 kg an hour, or 0.09 tonnes a day. The three numbers describe the same growth in different [units]{.hl}.

_Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica_
:::

## Changing units

```{r}
words <- words |> mutate(aoa_months = aoa * 12)

coef(lm(rt ~ aoa, data = words))
coef(lm(rt ~ aoa_months, data = words))
```

. . .

Multiply the predictor by 12, and the slope is divided by 12: `r round(b1 / 12, 2)` ms per month.

. . .

The line and its R² (`r round(r2, 2)`) stay the same; the numbers are just easier to read.

## Where is the intercept?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
ggplot(words, aes(x = aoa, y = rt)) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, alpha = 0.15, size = 1) +
  geom_abline(intercept = b0, slope = b1, colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = moss) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = b0, colour = hornbill, size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.4, y = b0, hjust = 0, colour = hornbill, size = 5.5,
           label = paste("intercept =", round(b0), "ms at age 0")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 18)) +
  labs(x = "Age of acquisition (years)", y = "Reaction time (ms)")
```

The intercept is where the line crosses x = 0: far outside the data.

## Centring {.smaller}

[Centring]{.hl} subtracts the mean, so that 0 means "a word of average age of acquisition":

```{r}
words <- words |>
  mutate(aoa_c = aoa - mean(aoa))

coef(lm(rt ~ aoa_c, data = words))
mean(words$rt)
```

. . .

The slope does not change. The intercept is now the mean reaction time: the predicted value for a word of average age of acquisition.

## Centring

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
ggplot(words, aes(x = aoa_c, y = rt)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = moss) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, alpha = 0.15, size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = hornbill, fill = hornbill, linewidth = 1.4) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = mean(words$rt), colour = mist, size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Age of acquisition (years), centred: 0 = average", y = "Reaction time (ms)")
```

The data and the line are unchanged, and only the `x` axis has moved. The intercept (white) sits in the middle of the data.

## Centre on any meaningful value {.smaller}

The mean is not the only choice. Subtract any value that makes 0 meaningful:

```{r}
words <- words |> mutate(aoa_6 = aoa - 6)
coef(lm(rt ~ aoa_6, data = words))
```

. . .

The intercept is now the predicted reaction time for a word learned at age 6, when most children start school.

. . .

In linguistic data:

| Centred predictor | The intercept describes |
|:--|:--|
| `age - 18` | an 18-year-old speaker |
| `year - 2000` | the year 2000 |
| `trial - 1` | the first trial |

## Standardising

[Standardising]{.hl} turns values into [z-scores]{.hl}: subtract the mean, then divide by the standard deviation.

::: {.formula}
z = (x − mean) / SD
:::

```{r}
words <- words |>
  mutate(aoa_z = (aoa - mean(aoa)) / sd(aoa))

coef(lm(rt ~ aoa_z, data = words))
```

. . .

The slope is now the change in reaction time for a word acquired one standard deviation later.

## What a z-score says

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
aoa_m <- mean(words$aoa); aoa_s <- sd(words$aoa)
ggplot(words, aes(x = aoa)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = kingfisher, colour = floor_col, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = aoa_m + (-2:2) * aoa_s, colour = hornbill, linetype = c("dotted", "dotted", "solid", "dotted", "dotted")) +
  annotate("label", x = aoa_m + (-2:2) * aoa_s, y = Inf, vjust = 1.3, label = paste("z =", -2:2),
           fill = floor_col, colour = hornbill, label.size = 0, size = 4.5) +
  labs(x = "Age of acquisition (years)", y = "Count")
```

A z-score says how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean: z = 0 is average, z = −2 is two SDs below it. From lecture 3, about 95% of values in a normal distribution lie between z = −2 and z = 2.

## Comparing predictors {.smaller}

Which predicts reaction time more strongly: age of acquisition (years) or word length (letters)?

```{r}
c(coef(lm(rt ~ aoa, data = words))[2],
  coef(lm(rt ~ length, data = words))[2])
```

. . .

Years and letters cannot be compared. Standardise both. `scale()` computes z-scores, but returns a matrix, so wrap it in `as.numeric()`:

```{r}
words <- words |> mutate(length_z = as.numeric(scale(length)))
c(coef(lm(rt ~ aoa_z, data = words))[2],
  coef(lm(rt ~ length_z, data = words))[2])
```

. . .

In raw units, length looked slightly stronger. Per standard deviation, age of acquisition goes with the larger change in reaction time.

## Speaker normalisation {.smaller}

Vowel formants are a classic linguistic use of z-scores, in [speaker normalisation]{.hl}.

. . .

Speakers with longer vocal tracts have lower formants overall. Raw F1 and F2 mix up which vowel and which speaker.

```{r}
formants
```

`formants`: 20 tokens of /i a u/ from each of two speakers. Every formant of speaker B is 1.2 times the same formant of speaker A.

## Raw formants

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.6
ggplot(formants, aes(x = f2, y = f1, colour = speaker, shape = vowel)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_reverse() + scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "F2 (Hz)", y = "F1 (Hz)", colour = "Speaker", shape = "Vowel") +
  guides(shape = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = mist)))
```

The same vowels from two speakers land in different places.

## Lobanov normalisation

z-score each formant within each speaker (Lobanov, 1971). With `.by` from lecture 2:

```{r}
formants_z <- formants |>
  mutate(across(c(f1, f2), \(x) as.numeric(scale(x))),
         .by = speaker)
```

. . .

`.by = speaker`: each speaker's F1 and F2 are z-scored using that speaker's own mean and SD.

## After normalisation

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.4
ggplot(formants_z, aes(x = f2, y = f1, colour = speaker, shape = vowel)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_reverse() + scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "F2 (z, within speaker)", y = "F1 (z, within speaker)",
       colour = "Speaker", shape = "Vowel") +
  guides(shape = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = mist)))
```

After normalisation, the vowels overlap across speakers.

## Discussion

Lobanov normalisation removes the differences between speakers, so that vowels can be compared across them.

- When could those differences be exactly what you want to study?
- What would you lose by normalising in that case?

## Linear transformations: summary {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
fit <- function(f) coef(lm(f, data = words))
tibble(
  predictor = c("aoa", "aoa_months", "aoa_c", "aoa_6", "aoa_z"),
  `0 means` = c("age 0", "age 0", "average age of acquisition", "age 6", "average age of acquisition"),
  intercept = c(fit(rt ~ aoa)[1], fit(rt ~ aoa_months)[1], fit(rt ~ aoa_c)[1],
                fit(rt ~ aoa_6)[1], fit(rt ~ aoa_z)[1]),
  slope = c(fit(rt ~ aoa)[2], fit(rt ~ aoa_months)[2], fit(rt ~ aoa_c)[2],
                fit(rt ~ aoa_6)[2], fit(rt ~ aoa_z)[2]),
  `slope per` = c("1 year", "1 month", "1 year", "1 year", "1 SD"),
  R2 = round(r2, 2)
) |>
  mutate(across(intercept:slope, \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

. . .

Linear transformations change what the numbers mean, while the fit stays the same.

# Correlation

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the [heart]{.hl} of a blue whale that washed ashore in Newfoundland, Canada, in 2014 weighed about 180 kg. It is now on display at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto.

_Source: Royal Ontario Museum_
:::

## Pearson's r {.smaller}

The [correlation coefficient]{.hl} r measures how closely two variables follow a straight line.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
set.seed(2)
make_r <- function(r, n = 150) {
  x <- rnorm(n); y <- r * x + sqrt(1 - r^2) * rnorm(n)
  tibble(x, y, label = paste("r =", r))
}
bind_rows(make_r(-0.8), make_r(0), make_r(0.4), make_r(0.9)) |>
  mutate(label = fct_inorder(label)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.6, size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ label, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())
```

- From -1 (perfect negative) through 0 (no linear relation) to +1 (perfect positive)
- It has no units: it is the same whether you measure in years, months or days

## Computing correlations with `cor()` {.smaller}

```{r}
cor(words$rt, words$aoa)
```

. . .

`language_attitudes`: 320 respondents rate dialect speakers on 1 to 5 scales. Some respondents skipped items, so those cells are `NA`:

```{r}
cor(language_attitudes$friendly, language_attitudes$warm)
```

. . .

As with `mean()` in lecture 2, one `NA` makes the whole result `NA`. In `cor()`, the argument is `use = "complete.obs"`, which keeps only the respondents who answered both items:

```{r}
cor(language_attitudes$friendly, language_attitudes$warm, use = "complete.obs")
```

## Correlations per group

Per group, with `summarise()` and `.by`:

```{r}
language_attitudes |>
  summarise(r = cor(friendly, warm, use = "complete.obs"), .by = dialect_speaker)
```

## Correlation and regression {.smaller}

Standardise both variables, and the regression slope is the correlation:

```{r}
words <- words |> mutate(rt_z = as.numeric(scale(rt)))

coef(lm(rt_z ~ aoa_z, data = words))
cor(words$rt, words$aoa)
```

. . .

And in simple regression, R² = r²:

```{r}
cor(words$rt, words$aoa)^2
glance(m)$r.squared
```

## Anscombe's quartet {.smaller}

Anscombe (1973) built four data sets, available in R as `anscombe`:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
quartet <- anscombe |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c(".value", "set"), names_pattern = "(.)(.)") |>
  mutate(set = paste("Data set", set))

quartet_r <- quartet |>
  summarise(r = cor(x, y), .by = set) |>
  mutate(label = paste("r =", round(r, 2)))

ggplot(quartet, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1, fullrange = TRUE) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = quartet_r, aes(x = 5, y = 12.5, label = label),
            colour = mist, hjust = 0, size = 5) +
  facet_wrap(~ set, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

Four data sets with the same means, the same regression line and the same correlation, r = 0.82. Only one of them looks like a straight-line relationship, which is why you should plot the data before you trust r.

## Correlation by group {.smaller}

F1 and F2 in the formant data:

```{r}
cor(formants$f1, formants$f2)
formants |> summarise(r = cor(f1, f2), .by = vowel)
```

. . .

Negative overall, positive within every vowel: Simpson's paradox, as with last week's penguins. Across vowels, a high F1 goes with a low F2 (/a/ against /i/). Within a vowel, speaker B has both formants higher. A correlation describes only the data you give it, and says nothing about the process behind them.

## Correlation and causation

In children, shoe size and vocabulary size are correlated: children with bigger feet tend to know more words.

. . .

Foot size has no effect on vocabulary. Both grow with a [third variable]{.hl}, age.

. . .

A correlation, or a regression slope, tells us that two variables go together. Whether one causes the other is a question for the design of the study.

## Discussion

Suppose children who are read to at home every day know more words than children who are not.

- Does reading aloud cause vocabulary growth? What else could explain the correlation?
- What kind of study would let you decide?

# Logarithms

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` blue whale calls can reach 188 decibels. Decibels are a [logarithmic scale]{.hl}: every 10 dB more means ten times the sound intensity.

_Source: WWF_
:::

## Orders of magnitude {.smaller}

Some linguistic variables span many orders of magnitude. Word frequency is the classic example:

```{r}
zipf_rt
range(zipf_rt$freq)
```

. . .

`zipf_rt`: 2000 words with their frequency per million words and a lexical decision time (`rt`, in ms). The most frequent word is about `r round(max(zipf_rt$freq) / min(zipf_rt$freq))` times more frequent than the least frequent one.

## What is a logarithm? {.smaller}

A [logarithm]{.hl} answers one question: how many times do I multiply the base by itself to get this number? `log10(1000)` is 3, because 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000.

. . .

So the log turns multiplying into adding: each step of 1 on the log scale is one more multiplication by the base.

. . .

```{r}
log10(1000)
log2(8)
log(exp(2))
exp(log(50))
```

`log()` is the natural log, with base e ≈ 2.718, and `exp()` undoes it.

## Which base?

| Function | Base | One unit means |
|---|---|---|
| `log10()` | 10 | a tenfold increase |
| `log2()` | 2 | a doubling |
| `log()` | e ≈ 2.718 | the default in R and in most models |

. . .

The base changes only the numbers on the axis, and the shape stays the same: `log10(x)` is just `log(x) / log(10)`. Choose the base that is easiest to explain.

## Zeros and negatives

```{r}
log(0)
log(-5)
```

. . .

The log is only defined for positive numbers.

. . .

Frequency counts often contain zeros (a word that never occurs in a corpus). A common fix is to add 1 first. `log1p(x)` is the same as `log(x + 1)`:

```{r}
log1p(c(0, 9, 99))
```

## Logging a predictor

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
bind_rows(
  mutate(zipf_rt, x = freq, scale = "Raw frequency"),
  mutate(zipf_rt, x = log10(freq), scale = "log10(frequency)")
) |>
  mutate(scale = fct_inorder(scale)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = rt)) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.3, size = 1.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.2, se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Reaction time (ms)")
```

On the raw scale, most words are squeezed against zero and a straight line fits badly. On the log scale, the relationship is close to linear.

## Logging a predictor

```{r}
m_freq <- lm(rt ~ log10(freq), data = zipf_rt)
coef(m_freq)
```

. . .

Each tenfold increase in frequency (10 → 100 → 1000) goes with responses about `r round(-coef(m_freq)[2])` ms faster.

. . .

Frequency effects in language are usually [multiplicative]{.hl}: going from 10 to 100 matters about as much as going from 100,000 to 1,000,000.

## Logging the outcome {.smaller}

Reaction times are positive and [right-skewed]{.hl} (lecture 3). So are the residuals of a model fitted to raw RTs:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.8
m_log <- lm(log(rt) ~ log10(freq), data = zipf_rt)

bind_rows(
  tibble(model = "lm(rt ~ log10(freq))", resid = as.numeric(scale(residuals(m_freq)))),
  tibble(model = "lm(log(rt) ~ log10(freq))", resid = as.numeric(scale(residuals(m_log))))
) |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = resid, fill = model)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, colour = floor_col) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(orchid, pandan)) +
  labs(x = "Residuals (z-scored)", y = "Count") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

After the log, the residuals are much more symmetric: closer to what the linear model assumes (lecture 4).

## Reading a log outcome {.smaller}

```{r}
m_log <- lm(log(rt) ~ log10(freq), data = zipf_rt)
coef(m_log)
exp(coef(m_log)[2])
```

. . .

On the log scale, effects multiply. Each tenfold increase in frequency multiplies the RT by `r round(exp(coef(m_log)[2]), 3)`: responses about `r round((1 - exp(coef(m_log)[2])) * 100, 1)`% faster.

. . .

Back to milliseconds with `exp()`:

```{r}
exp(predict(m_log, newdata = tibble(freq = c(1, 10, 100, 1000))))
```

## When to log

- The variable is positive and [right-skewed]{.hl}: RTs, durations, frequencies, counts
- Effects are plausibly [multiplicative]{.hl}: "x% faster" rather than "x ms faster"
- The residuals of the raw model are skewed or funnel-shaped

. . .

A log transformation does not fix every problem. Report which variables you transformed and why, and interpret the coefficients on the transformed scale.

# The word "normalising"

## Kinds of normalising {.smaller}

"Normalising" is used for several different operations:

| What people mean | What it does |
|:--|:--|
| z-scoring | subtracts the mean and divides by the SD |
| min-max scaling | squeezes values into the range 0 to 1 |
| a normalising transformation | makes a distribution look more normal, e.g. a log |
| speaker normalisation | removes vocal tract differences in phonetics, e.g. Lobanov |

. . .

Min-max scaling in R:

```{r}
x <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42)
(x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x))
```

. . .

In your write-up, avoid the word on its own. Say exactly what you did: "F1 and F2 were z-scored within speaker (Lobanov, 1971)". See also Winter (2019), section 5.7.

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- Changing units and [centring]{.hl} change what the intercept and slope mean, and the fit stays the same
- [Standardising]{.hl} puts variables on a common scale, with slopes per SD
- [Correlation]{.hl} is the slope between two z-scored variables: unitless, from −1 to 1
- The same r can come from very different data, so plot the data too
- [Logarithms]{.hl} turn multiplicative effects into additive ones, and reduce skew
- Name your transformation precisely, instead of just writing "normalised"
:::
